title: Cross out one exact row: Iceberg position deletes
goal: See how a file path plus a zero-based row position hides one row without rewriting the whole data file.
tag: Foundation · Iceberg v2 mechanism with a v3 boundary
concept:
A warehouse file contains three orders: O10, O11, and O12. You need to remove O11. Rewriting the whole file works, but it can be expensive. A smaller option is to publish a separate note that says: “in this exact file, hide row 1.”

That note is a position delete. It identifies a row with two values: the data file path and the row’s position inside that file. Positions start at zero, so O11 is position 1. Readers combine the data file and its applicable delete records to produce the visible table.

orders-A.parquet

0 → O10
1 → O11
2 → O12

Delete record

file = orders-A.parquet
position = 1

Visible rows

O10
O11
O12

The file name matters. Position 1 in orders-B.parquet is a different row. The snapshot metadata tells a reader which data files and delete files belong together.
example:
The reader scans A. For every row it asks whether (file_path, position) appears in the delete set. The pair (orders-A.parquet, 1) matches O11, so the reader skips it. O10 and O12 remain.

deleted = (file_path, row_position) in position_deletes
if not deleted:
    return row

If the data file is rewritten, row positions can change. A maintenance operation must publish new snapshot metadata and reconcile applicable deletes; copying the old number onto an unrelated file can delete the wrong row.

Version boundary: Iceberg v2 introduced row-level delete files. In v3, new position delete files are prohibited in favor of deletion vectors, although existing position delete files remain valid after an upgrade.
practice: Predict which order disappears. Change the file and position, then compare the visible rows in both files.
boundary: A small snapshot-aware reader over two in-memory files. It does not parse Iceberg manifests, sequence numbers, Parquet, equality deletes, deletion vectors, compaction, or engine compatibility. Never apply a position without the exact file identity and snapshot rules.
questions: Which pair hides O11 in the example?
orders-A.parquet and position 1
orders-A.parquet and position 2
Any file and position 1
Positions start at zero, and the file path is part of the identity. O11 is row 1 only in orders-A.parquet.
Why is position 1 alone unsafe?
Positions are encrypted
Each data file has its own position 1
Iceberg rows never have positions
The same number names a different row in every file. A position delete needs the exact data file path too.
What changes for an Iceberg v3 writer?
It should add new position delete files
It must ignore all existing deletes
It uses deletion vectors for new position deletes; existing v2 files can remain valid
The specification prohibits adding new position delete files to v3 tables and retains existing ones from upgraded v2 tables.
written_questions: Explain why the file path and row position must travel together.
A compaction rewrites orders-A.parquet. What must be reconciled before publishing the new snapshot?
sources: Apache Iceberg table specification: delete formats
Living specification; v2/v3 delete requirements reviewed

steps.note: Start with two files. Each file numbers its own rows from zero.
Create one marker for row 1 in file A.
The reader removes only a row whose file and position both match.
Position 1 in file B is O21, proving that the number alone is not an identity.

walkthrough.limit: Executes pair matching over Python lists. It does not read an Iceberg table or model snapshot sequence rules.

title: One fetch, many callers: request coalescing
goal: Let concurrent callers for the same key share one in-flight operation without pretending it is a persistent cache.
concept:
Three checkout requests ask for the same price at nearly the same time. If all three call the slow catalog service, one burst becomes three identical calls. Instead, the first caller starts the fetch. The other two wait for that same result.

This is request coalescing, often called singleflight: one operation is in flight for a key at a time. Callers for a different key may run in parallel.

Caller A · MUG

Starts the catalog fetch

Caller B · MUG

Waits for A

Caller C · PLATE

Starts a separate fetch

MUG → one shared result · PLATE → another result

It is not a lasting cache. After the MUG fetch finishes and leaves the in-flight map, a later MUG request may call the catalog again.
example:
At time 0, A asks for MUG and becomes the leader. At time 1, B asks for MUG and becomes a waiter. At time 2, C asks for PLATE and becomes another leader because the key differs. When MUG finishes, A and B receive the same value.

value, error, shared = group.do(key, load)

The result includes failures. If the leader times out, current waiters see that same error. Coalescing reduces duplicate load; it does not make an unreliable dependency reliable. Add appropriate deadlines, retry policy, and a real cache separately.
practice: Choose three request keys and decide whether the loader succeeds. Predict the number of actual loads before running the batch.
boundary: A deterministic batch model, not real threads. It groups requests that overlap in one teaching window. It omits cancellation, per-caller deadlines, memory cleanup, retries, cache TTLs, and fairness. A shared error is still an error.
questions: A and B request MUG together; C requests PLATE. How many loads start?
One
Two
Three
One MUG leader and one PLATE leader run. Only callers with the same key share work.
The MUG leader times out. What do current MUG waiters receive?
The same timeout result
A guaranteed success
A stale value from singleflight
Waiters receive the original call's result, including its error. Singleflight is not a cache or retry engine.
A new MUG request arrives after the first call finished. What is guaranteed?
It always reuses the old result
It may start a new load
It is rejected forever
Once no call is in flight, coalescing alone retains no persistent value. A later request may execute again.
written_questions: Explain why coalescing by product key reduces a burst without serializing every product.
What per-caller deadline problem appears when one slow leader has many waiters?

steps.note: Three callers overlap; two use the same key.
The first occurrence of each key becomes a leader.
Only two underlying loads run: MUG and PLATE.

steps.code:
results = [f"price:{key}" for key in requests]
shared = [requests.count(key) > 1 for key in requests]
steps.note: Both MUG callers receive the same logical result; PLATE is not shared.

walkthrough.limit: Executes grouping, not concurrent threads. It demonstrates key scope and shared results only.

title: Keep serving with the last good map: control plane vs data plane
goal: Separate configuration changes from request serving so existing traffic can continue during a control-plane outage.
concept:
A restaurant has a printed seating map. The manager updates the map; hosts use the latest approved copy to seat guests. If the manager’s laptop fails, hosts cannot accept a new layout—but they can keep seating guests with the last good map.

The manager’s work is the control plane: create or change configuration. Seating guests is the data plane: do the daily work using that configuration.

Control plane

Propose route changes
Validate and publish

Last good snapshot

orders → cell-a
payments → cell-b

Data plane

Route every request locally

The key is not merely two boxes. The serving path has a local, durable-enough copy of everything it needs. An outage can delay updates without stopping already-working routes.
example:
The route snapshot says orders → cell-a. A request arrives while the control plane is healthy: the data plane reads its local snapshot and routes to cell-a. Now publishing goes down. A proposed move to cell-c cannot be accepted, but orders still go to cell-a.

The broken design asks the control plane where to send every request. That turns a configuration outage into a customer outage.

route = last_good_snapshot[service]  # serving path
publish(candidate)                    # change path

This is a deeper static-stability installment: survive with pre-positioned state first; repair or change the state after the control plane recovers.
practice: Toggle the control plane, route requests, and attempt a change. Then enable the broken per-request dependency and observe the blast radius.
boundary: A route-table decision model. It omits stale-state limits, leases, authentication, propagation, split brain, endpoint health, capacity, rollback, and emergency change channels. Some control-plane failures require data-plane fail-closed behavior for safety.
sim:
Last good route

Request result
questions: The control plane fails after cell-a was published. In the stable design, where does the next order go?
cell-a
Nowhere
A random cell
The data plane keeps the last good snapshot and continues using the known route.
Which operation should fail during the outage?
Every existing request
Publishing the new cell-c route
Reading the local route
Changes require the control plane. Existing data-plane work should not take that dependency when static stability is the goal.
When might serving the old snapshot be unsafe?
When policy requires an immediate revoke
Whenever the route has a name
Only on Tuesdays
Some security or safety changes must take effect immediately. The architecture needs an explicit staleness and fail-closed policy.
written_questions: Explain the difference between delayed change and failed service in this example.
Name one control-plane fact your data plane must pre-position before an outage.
sources: AWS Builders' Library: Static stability using Availability Zones

steps.note: Start with one published route and a healthy change path.
Serving reads the local snapshot, not the publisher.
The publisher fails, so the proposed route is not accepted.
The next request still uses cell-a and succeeds in this bounded model.

walkthrough.limit: Executes a dictionary lookup. It proves no availability target and models neither endpoint health nor state propagation.

title: Follow one agent run: parent and child spans
goal: Trace an agent, model call, and tool call as one tree so a failure points to the responsible step.
tag: New development · OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions are Development
concept:
An order-support agent says “I could not answer.” A single success/failure log does not tell you whether the model chose a bad tool, the tool timed out, or the final model call ignored the tool result.

A trace is the whole journey of one run. A span is one timed step inside it. Give the agent invocation a parent span. Put model and tool operations underneath as child spans. Then the tree preserves order, duration, and error location.

invoke_agent · 120 ms

trace t-42
parent: none

chat · 45 ms

parent: agent
chooses lookup

execute_tool · ERROR

parent: agent
timeout

This is harness engineering: the run is observable without trusting the agent’s own summary. The trace does not prove the answer is correct; it tells you where to investigate and supplies data for evaluation.
example:
The root span is invoke_agent order_support. A child chat span asks the model what to do. A child execute_tool order_lookup records a timeout. The root then ends with an error. Because every child has the same trace ID and the correct parent ID, the UI can reconstruct one tree.

agent = start_span("invoke_agent", trace="t-42")
tool  = start_span("execute_tool", parent=agent.id)
tool.error_type = "timeout"

Record low-cardinality error types and operational metadata. Treat prompts, outputs, tool arguments, and customer IDs as sensitive. The OpenTelemetry GenAI agent conventions are still marked Development, so pin the semantic-convention version and expect change.
practice: Toggle a tool failure and a missing parent link. Predict whether the trace still shows one useful tree.
boundary: A small trace-tree validator. It does not send telemetry, sample traces, redact real content, measure tokens, or implement an OpenTelemetry SDK. A good trace proves observability structure, not answer correctness, deterministic replay, or privacy compliance.
questions: The tool span has no parent ID. What is the immediate observability problem?
The tool becomes faster
The run appears as multiple roots instead of one tree
The model output becomes correct
Without the link, the trace cannot reliably show that the tool belonged to this agent run.
Where should a tool timeout appear?
Only in the agent's natural-language reply
On the tool span with a low-cardinality error type
As a new conversation ID
The responsible span should record the error. A trace is operational evidence, not a narration by the model.
No real conversation identifier exists. What should instrumentation do?
Hash the prompt
Reuse the trace ID as conversation ID
Leave conversation ID absent
The current conventions say not to invent a UUID, trace ID, or content hash as a fallback conversation ID.
written_questions: Explain how the span tree separates a model decision from a tool failure.
Which fields would you redact or omit before tracing a production order-support agent?
sources: OpenTelemetry: Semantic conventions for GenAI agent and framework spans

steps.note: Start one synthetic trace with no spans.
Create the agent root span.
The model call is a child and completed normally.

steps.code:
spans.append({"id": "s3", "name": "execute_tool", "parent": "s1", "status": "ERROR", "error.type": "timeout"})
failed_span = next(s["name"] for s in spans if s["status"] == "ERROR" and s["parent"] is not None)
steps.note: The child tool span localizes the operational failure.

walkthrough.limit: Builds plain dictionaries. It does not use an OpenTelemetry SDK or export real telemetry.

title: Report changes, not every frame: amplitude-tunable event photosensing
goal: Understand the paper's reported combination of temporal-contrast events and tunable signal amplitude, without treating a toy model as device physics.
tag: Research claim · Nature Materials article published 2026-09-30
concept:
A normal camera repeatedly sends the whole scene, even when nothing changes. An event sensor is more like a motion-sensitive doorbell: it speaks when brightness changes. The new research asks for one more capability—make the event louder or quieter using a programmable gain.

The paper reports an organic mixed ionic–electronic photosensor that combines temporal-contrast detection and analogue amplitude control in one active layer. Fast electronic response produces a spike; ionic-mediated inhibition adjusts the spike amplitude.

Light stays at 10

No change
No event

Light jumps 10 → 40

Change = 30
Event produced

Inhibition = 50%

Toy amplitude
30 → 15

That last arithmetic is our analogy, not the paper’s device equation. It makes “change detection plus adjustable amplitude” visible without pretending to reproduce ionic and electronic transport.
example:
Our toy sensor remembers the previous brightness. A new sample at the same value produces zero. A jump from 10 to 40 produces a raw contrast of 30. With 50% inhibition, the displayed amplitude is 15.

contrast = abs(current - previous)
event = max(0, contrast - threshold)
amplitude = event * (1 - inhibition)

The research article reports device measurements and device-informed simulations for neuromorphic vision. It does not establish a commercial camera, production energy guarantee, or general-purpose vision accuracy. Read the primary paper for materials, protocol, and benchmark details.
practice: Sample a stable light level, then create a jump. Change inhibition and explain why event timing stays the same while this toy amplitude changes.
boundary: An original difference-and-gain analogy. It does not model the organic material, ions, charge transport, device time constants, noise, polarity, energy, arrays, or the paper's experimental curves. Numeric outputs are synthetic, not reproduced measurements.
sim:
Previous → current

Toy event amplitude
questions: Brightness remains 40 on the next sample. What does the toy produce?
A new 40-unit event
No change event
A guaranteed negative spike
The toy compares current with previous. Equal values have zero contrast, so no event crosses the threshold.
What does increasing inhibition change in this lesson's analogy?
The event amplitude
The publication date
The previous brightness
Inhibition scales the synthetic amplitude after change detection. It does not change the stored previous sample.
Which claim is justified?
The lab reproduces the material physics
The paper reports a single-active-layer organic sensor with temporal contrast and adjustable amplitude
The device is already a production camera
That is the bounded research claim from the primary article. The browser model is explicitly only an analogy.
written_questions: Explain why an event sensor can avoid sending repeated unchanged frames.
Which device evidence would you inspect before comparing this research with a commercial event camera?
sources: Zhao et al.: Amplitude-controllable event-driven organic photosensors based on ionic-mediated inhibition
Nature Materials; published 2026-09-30; open-access research article

steps.note: Use a small synthetic brightness stream and a 50% gain reduction.

steps.code: changes = [abs(b - a) for a, b in zip(samples, samples[1:])]
steps.note: Only differences between consecutive samples matter.

steps.code: events = [max(0, change - threshold) for change in changes]
steps.note: Small or absent changes are removed by the toy threshold.

steps.code: amplitudes = [round(event * (1 - inhibition), 1) for event in events]
steps.note: The remaining event amplitudes are reduced by the toy inhibition control.

walkthrough.limit: Executes an original arithmetic analogy. Values are not measurements and equations are not the paper's device model.

title: Speed aid or handoff record? Cache vs artifact
goal: Use a cache to make rebuilding faster and an artifact to carry the exact output a later job must consume.
concept:
A kitchen keeps common flour in a pantry and puts today’s finished cake in a labeled delivery box. Missing pantry flour is inconvenient—you can buy more. Missing the labeled cake means delivery cannot continue.

A CI cache is the pantry. It reuses dependencies or expensive intermediate files across runs to save time. A job must still work after a cache miss by downloading or regenerating them.

An artifact is the delivery box. It stores files produced by a job, such as a tested binary, report, or log. Another job can download that exact output.

Cache

npm packages
Keyed by lockfile
Miss → download again

Build job

Tests commit abc123
Produces app.zip

Artifact

app.zip from this run
Deploy downloads it
example:
Run 1 has no dependency cache, so dependencies download. The build creates app-abc123.zip and uploads it as an artifact. Deploy downloads that artifact.

Run 2 with the same lockfile may hit the cache and install faster, but it still builds a new artifact for the new commit. If the cache is absent, rebuild. If the required artifact is absent, stop deployment rather than rebuilding a possibly different output.

- uses: actions/cache@v4
  with:
    key: deps-${{ hashFiles('**/lockfile') }}
- uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
  with:
    name: tested-app
    path: app.zip

Restored caches are untrusted input. Never put secrets in them; use precise keys and low-trust workflow restrictions.
practice: Change the lockfile key, toggle artifact upload, and run build then deploy. Predict which missing object slows the pipeline and which blocks the handoff.
boundary: A local state machine, not a GitHub Actions run. It omits cache scopes, restore keys, retention, quotas, immutable artifact details, attestations, permissions, fork policies, and action-version pinning. No workflow is installed.
sim:
Dependency cache

Run artifact

Deploy
js: let caches=new Set(),artifact=null;function paint(msg='Ready'){cacheView.textContent=caches.has(lockKey.value)?'HIT '+lockKey.value:'MISS '+lockKey.value;artifactView.textContent=artifact??'none';deployView.textContent=msg;world.textContent='Cache miss may be regenerated. Required artifact missing blocks this deploy.';}runBuild.onclick=()=>{const hit=caches.has(lockKey.value);caches.add(lockKey.value);artifact=uploadArtifact.checked?'app-abc123.zip':null;paint(`Build success · dependencies ${hit?'restored':'downloaded'}`)};runDeploy.onclick=()=>paint(artifact?'DEPLOY '+artifact:'BLOCKED: tested artifact missing');resetPipeline.onclick=()=>{caches=new Set();artifact=null;paint()};lockKey.onchange=()=>paint();paint();
questions: The dependency cache misses. What should the build do?
Fail forever
Download or regenerate dependencies, then continue
Deploy an old binary
GitHub's guidance says jobs should be able to recreate cached files when the cache is unavailable.
Which object should carry the tested app.zip to deploy?
A workflow artifact
A secret
Only a dependency cache
Artifacts persist files produced by a job and pass them between jobs. They identify the run output being handed off.
Why treat a restored cache as untrusted?
Caches can never contain files
A readable or poisoned cache can influence later execution
Artifacts automatically encrypt every dependency
GitHub warns that cache contents may be read or poisoned across relevant scopes and low-trust triggers. Do not store secrets; validate what executes.
written_questions: Explain why a cache miss should cost time while a required artifact miss should stop deployment.
What would you include in a cache key for a Java or Node build, and why?
sources: Living official documentation; includes cache security guidance

steps.note: Start a run without a cache or artifact.

steps.code:
cache_hit = lock_key in cache
if not cache_hit:
    cache.add(lock_key)
dependencies = "ready"
steps.note: A cache miss triggers a download, then dependencies become ready.
The build creates the exact output for this synthetic commit.

steps.code:
deploy_input = artifact
deploy_ok = deploy_input is not None
steps.note: Deploy consumes the run artifact. It does not depend on the cache as the release handoff.

walkthrough.limit: Executes Python sets and strings. It does not call GitHub Actions, store files, or deploy anything.

title: Do not erase a newer edit: ETag and If-Match
goal: Make an update conditional on the version a client actually read so stale writes fail instead of silently winning.
concept:
Alice and Bob open the same order note. Both see “address: A” and version "v1". Alice changes the address to B. Bob, still looking at the old copy, changes the delivery window. If Bob sends the whole old document, he may erase Alice’s address.

An ETag is a server-provided identifier for a selected representation. The client sends its identifier back in If-Match: “apply my change only if the current version still matches what I read.”

Both GET

address A
ETag “v1”

Alice PUT

If-Match “v1”
address B → “v2”

Bob PUT

If-Match “v1”
412 · reread first

The rejection prevents a lost update: one client accidentally overwriting another client’s parallel work.
example:
Alice sends:

PUT /orders/42
If-Match: "v1"

{"address":"B","window":"morning"}

The server compares "v1" with its current ETag. They match, so it stores Alice’s representation and returns "v2". Bob later sends If-Match: "v1". It no longer matches, so the server does not perform the update and can return 412 Precondition Failed. Bob must GET v2, merge intentionally, and retry with the new ETag.

Use a strong validator for If-Match comparison. Define whether your ETag represents the full resource or a specific representation variant.
practice: Run Alice's update, then Bob's stale update. Turn off the condition to see how the newer address is silently overwritten.
boundary: A single-process whole-resource update model. It omits authentication, authorization, weak validators, content negotiation, PATCH merge rules, databases, replicas, retries, idempotency keys, and the RFC's already-applied success exception. Production servers need an atomic compare-and-update.
sim:
Server resource

Bob response
js:
let resource,etag,bobCopy,bobTag;function reset(){resource={address:'A',window:'morning'};etag='"v1"';bobCopy={...resource};bobTag=etag;paint('Bob has not written.')}function paint(msg){resourceView.textContent=`${JSON.stringify(resource)} · ETag ${etag}`;responseView.textContent=msg;world.textContent=`Bob read ${JSON.stringify(bobCopy)} with ${bobTag}
Current server is ${JSON.stringify(resource)} with ${etag}`;}aliceUpdate.onclick=()=>{resource={address:'B',window:'morning'};etag='"v2"';paint('Alice stored v2')};bobUpdate.onclick=()=>{if(useIfMatch.checked&&bobTag!==etag){paint('412 Precondition Failed · no write')}else{resource={...bobCopy,window:'evening'};etag='"v3"';paint('200 OK · Bob overwrote the whole resource')}};resetOrder.onclick=reset;reset();
questions: Alice has advanced the resource to v2. Bob sends If-Match v1. What happens?
Server applies Bob's stale copy
Server does not perform the update and may return 412
Server deletes the ETag
The condition is false. RFC 9110 says the origin server must not perform the requested method; 412 can report the failed precondition.
What problem does If-Match address here?
Lost updates between parallel editors
Slow DNS
Missing authentication
It stops a stale representation from silently overwriting a newer change. Authentication is a separate concern.
Why must compare and write be atomic at the server?
To avoid another write slipping between the check and update
To make ETags human-readable
To cache every response forever
A separate check followed later by a write recreates the race. The selected version must be compared as part of the update decision.
written_questions: Explain Bob's safe recovery after receiving 412.
How would partial PATCH semantics change the merge decision but not remove the need for concurrency control?
sources: RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics — ETag and If-Match

steps.code:
resource = {"address": "A", "window": "morning"}
etag = "v1"
bob_copy = resource.copy()
bob_tag = etag
steps.note: Both clients start from the same v1 representation.
Alice updates the address and the server advances the validator.
Bob's v1 tag does not match the current v2 tag.
The server returns 412 and leaves Alice's address intact.

walkthrough.limit: Executes an in-memory comparison. It does not implement an HTTP server or a database transaction.
